newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria shies away from radical economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria shies away from radical economic reforms.

text.p: Nigeria's military government on Saturday unveiled a much-delayed 1997 fiscal budget shorn of widely-expected radical reforms such as privatisation of state firms and unifying the dual exchange rate regime.

Military ruler General Sani Abacha, in a nationwide radio and television broadcast, said government needed more consultations before embarking on privatisation of state companies while the dual exchange rate in place would continue.
"The various options open to government will be closely examined by a high-powered committee before any privatisation exercise is embarked upon," Abacha said.
It was an anti-climax to widespread expectation before the budget that Abacha would announce that privatisation would commence full blast in 1997 and inject new life into a dull economy.

The issue has been at the forefront of discussion in business circles within and outside Nigeria since October when finance minister Anthony Ani announced that Nigeria was seriously considering selling its crude oil production joint ventures and privatising the oil refineries.
Nigeria, sub-Saharan Africa's biggest economy, has been in recession since 1993 when the country slid into crisis over annulment of an election that would have restored democracy.

Its relations with the West have deteriorated over alleged human rights violations, including the detention since 1994 of Moshood Abiola, the presumed winer of the annulled poll and the nation's slow pace of democratisation.
Abacha did not say anything new on the protracted political crisis but said his programme to hand over power to a democratically-elected president next year was going well.
He concentrated on the economy, saying free market policies in place since early 1995 have stabilised the exchange rate and other critical sectors.
"Most economic fundamentals moved in the desired direction...accordingly, the 1997 budget is a budget of economic growth and development," he said.
The World Bank and local business leaders have been pressing for privatisation, saying it would bring in badly-needed funds to stimulate real economic growth.
Ani had argued at a seminar in Lagos that "Privatisation will open our economy up for the foreign investment we very much need."
But official sources said he had failed to convince the ruling military council at a crucial budget meeting this week that it was desirable to embark on privatisation straight away.

Abacha said oil-dependent Nigeria hoped to earn some 18.8 percent more revenue in 1997 over last year and pledged that a huge surplus recorded last year would be pumped into productive sectors, especially in the rural area.
He announced a drop in Nigeria's foreign debt to $28.06 billion at the end of 1996 from $32.58 at the end of the 1995 and attributed this to "adroit debt management".
He did not give precise details of how the debt had been reduced, but official sources said this may have been through a verification exercise that had questioned the validity of some of the debt.
